title: [inductor] Multiple randint calls cause inconsistent RNG results between eager and compiled mode after fixing the rng seed
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug To reproduce: ```python import torch import torch._dynamo torch._inductor.config.fallback_random = True def fn(): torch.manual_seed(0) out = torch.randint(0, 100, (4,1), dtype=torch.int64) # Shape and integer range are not important. other = torch.randint(0, 100, (2,1), dtype=torch.int64) # No inconsistency if remove this line, although the value won't be returned. return out cfunc = torch.compile(fn, backend='inductor') torch.manual_seed(0) out1 = fn() torch.manual_seed(0) out2 = cfunc() print(f'{out1=}') ''' out1=tensor([[44], [39], [33], [60]]) ''' print(f'{out2=}') ''' out2=tensor([[33], [60], [63], [79]]) ''' torch.testing.assert_close(out1, out2, equal_nan=True) ``` Problem: RNG state is inconsistent between eager execution and torch.compile(backend='inductor') execution, even after explicitly resetting the seed with torch.manual_seed(0) before each run. The issue occurs when two randint calls are called inside the compiled function:the output of the first randint already differs between eager and compiled mode, even though the second randint result is not returned. After a few debugging, I notice that the following version does NOT trigger the inconsistency: ```python def fn(): torch.manual_seed(0) out = torch.randint(0, 100, (4,1), dtype=torch.int64) torch.manual_seed(0) # Extra seed reset before second randint other = torch.randint(0, 100, (2,1), dtype=torch.int64) return out ``` The only difference is an extra torch.manual_seed(0) before the second randint. This behavior is bit counterintuitive: We already set the seed before the first `randint`, and the second `randint` does not modify the returned value. However, without setting the second `randint`'s rng seed still causes the first randint output to mismatch between eager and compiled mode. Note that this inconsistency only occurs for `inductor` backend, but does not occur for `eager/aot_eager`backend. ### Error logs _No response_ ### Versions [pip3] torch==2.11.0.dev20260209+cpu [pip3] triton==3.6.0 [conda] torch 2.11.0.dev20260209+cpu pypi_0 pypi [conda] triton 3.6.0 pypi_0 pypi cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @pbelevich @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @muchulee8 @amjames @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo

title: CUDA target overloads not handling kwargs
issue_body_excerpt: <!-- Thanks for opening an issue! To help the Numba team handle your information efficiently, please first ensure that there is no other issue present that already describes the issue you have (search at https://github.com/numba/numba/issues?&q=is%3Aissue). --> ## Reporting a bug <!-- Before submitting a bug report please ensure that you can check off these boxes: --> - [x] I have tried using the latest released version of Numba (most recent is visible in the change log (https://github.com/numba/numba/blob/main/CHANGE_LOG). - [x] I have included a self contained code sample to reproduce the problem. i.e. it's possible to run as 'python bug.py'. This: ```python import numpy as np from numba.cuda import jit from numba.extending import overload def bar(): pass @overload(bar, target='cuda') def ol_bar(x, kw1=None): def impl(x, kw1=None): return 123 return impl @jit def foo(arr): arr[0] = bar(2) tmp = np.zeros((1,)) foo[1, 1](tmp) print(tmp) ``` Fails typing with `TypeError("Signature mismatch: 1 argument types given, but function takes 2 arguments")`.
comments_excerpt: The issue seems to be that kwargs aren't considered when producing the args for compilation, this patch seems to fix it: ```diff diff --git a/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py b/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py --- a/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py +++ b/numba/cuda/dispatcher.py @@ -763,6 +763,7 @@ class CUDADispatcher(Dispatcher, serialize.ReduceMixin): # Ensure an exactly-matching overload is available if we can # compile. We proceed with the typing even if we can't compile # because we may be able to force a cast on the caller side. + pysig, args = self._compiler.fold_argument_types(args, kws) if self._can_compile: self.compile_device(tuple(args)) ``` cf. `_DispatcherBase` https://github.com/numba/numba/blob/f4b6fe0124fa7734ba2bb28c7685db5b6306c486/numba/core/dispatcher.py#L359 Notes from triage meeting: - There was a PR that attempted to add kwargs to CUDA, but I wasn't in support of the approach there, because it deviates from the core kwargs mechanism (#7871) - The above patch makes it look like argument folding works, but IIRC it will be incorrect if kwargs are in a different order in the parameter list to those in the declaration. I had an experiment with folding args (using a slightly different method to enable it) in https://github.com/gmarkall/numba/commit/1db1c44be1a541e73269ba12131762891d8410f5 Given that it is hard to make it work in general and maintain parity with the core dispatcher, we probably want to prevent kwargs being used for CUDA overloads. Some additional notes from an OOB discussion. The above one-line patch in https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/8528#issuecomment-1286983427 would potentially "fix" the use of `kwargs` when calling from device to device. Some investigation is needed into whether this is indeed the case.

title: Support For CPU Atomics
issue_body_excerpt: ## Feature request It would be great if there were a way to use atomic operations from within numba. Currently atomic operations are only supported when generating cuda or HSA code. I'm currently experimenting with using numba to write callbacks that are provided to a C++ concurrency library. In this context, atomics are useful in that they can reduce the amount of synchronization required (or to write the locks that are actually being used). You can technically use atomic operations now if you hide them inside a function pointer exported from C++, but the performance impacts of doing so aren't clear to me. At first glance, preventing inlining seems like a high price to pay for every atomic operation. With regards to what would be the most useful, weak memory consistency is by far the most common thing that shows up in the applications I'm looking at right now, but what's needed is application specific in general. Other consistencies could potentially be useful to me for being able to acquire/release existing locks without having to route everything through an externally compiled function, but that's more of a secondary concern at the moment.

Neat example! I hadn't seen that before. To document a use case for this feature: the [HogWild! algorithm](http://papers.nips.cc/paper/4390-hogwild-a-lock-free-approach-to-parallelizing-stochastic-gradient-descent) requires atomic floating-point addition. While that may be achievable in Numba's CUDA support, we need atomic intrinsics (ideally applicable to NumPy arrays, an intrinsic atomic `arr[i] += x` operation) in order to make such implementations that work without a GPU. Just wanted to add to this, I’ve felt a need for this when I wanted to: * generate large histograms in parallel (too large to give each thread a copy) * perform GraphBLAS-like parallel graph computations Yep, my use-cases involve parallel graph analytics as well. Adding another request for CPU atomics. I'm not sure how multi-dimensional cases are handled, but abstractly if there was an `atomic_add(arr, indx, val)` `atomic_compare_and_swap(arr, index, expected, new)` and an `atomig_get(arr, index)` that would be enough for me to work around a lack of other operations and get stuff working. This would let me get some [n-gram based](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.00200) parallel computing working and be enough for a lot of common workloads like Hogwild. voting up! Something like CUDA's atomicAdd, atomicMin, etc would be helpful. For the OMP hackend, the ``#pragma omp atomic`` should be of some help? I attempted to write an atomic add using `@intrinsic` about it is held up by https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/6920.

title: [RFC] Optimize persistent reduction with `recompute from cached inputs`
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch **1. Backgroud:** For normalization kernels, e.g. RMS Norm, the inputs are loaded twice, one for reduction, the other for normalization. Inductor generates a persistent reduction which loads inputs to registers for once and cache as float32 for computations. Due to register pressure, this feature is only used when the reduction dimension is small, e.g. <= 1024. [Recent blog](https://pytorch.org/blog/sota-normalization-performance-with-torch-compile/) showed the current SOTA is about 6000GB/s while the max on GB200 is about 7928 GB/s. **2. Proposal: Optimize persistent reduction with recompute from cached inputs** **2. 1 Register cache** (a) Instead of cache inputs as float32, we directly cache them as float16 and only convert to float32 at the time of computation. (b) Issue multiple load instructions at the same time to ensure enough bytes-in-flights The final generate kernel (using 2 unrolled loads as an example) should look like: ``` @triton.jit def rmsnorm_2tile_kernel(x_ptr, w_ptr, y_ptr, M, stride_x, stride_y, EPS: tl.constexpr, TILE: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr): pid = tl.program_id(0) rows = pid * BLOCK_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)[:, None] # [BLOCK_M, 1] mask = rows < M offs = tl.arange(0, TILE)[None, :] # [1, TILE] base = x_ptr + rows * stride_x x0 = tl.load(base + offs, mask=mask, other=0.0) x1 = tl.load(base + TILE + offs, mask=mask, other=0.0) ss = x0.to(tl.float32) * x0.to(tl.float32) ss += x1.to(tl.float32) * x1.to(tl.float32) inv_rms = tl.rsqrt(tl.sum(ss, axis=1)[:, None] / (2 * TILE) + EPS) ybase = y_ptr + rows * stride_y w0 = tl.load(w_ptr + offs) tl.store(ybase + offs, (x0.to(tl.float32) * inv_rms * w0).to(tl.bfloat16), mask=mask) w1 = tl.load(w_ptr + TILE + offs) tl.store(ybase + TILE + offs, (x1.to(tl.float32) * inv_rms * w1).to(tl.bfloat16), mask=mask) ``` **2.2 Shared memory cache with TMA** Register cache still suffers from register pressure when hidden size is larger than 8192, shared memory can be used, which can also benefit from cluster reduction where multiple SMs are used for one reduction row. **3. Preliminary Results:** SOL% = achieved bandwidth / 7928 GB/s peak. Measured with `torch.profiler (CUPTI)` and `L2 cache clearing`. Baseline is: `torch.compile(rms_norm_ref, mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs", fullgraph=True)` **3.1 Register cache** (best gains at common LLM hidden dims): | Shape (M × N) | Baseline | Reg-tiled | Improvement | |----------------|----------|-----------|-------------| | 8192 × 8192 | 71.8% | **94.2%** | **+22.4pp** | | 16384 × 4096 | 80.8% | **97.4%** | **+16.6pp** | | 32768 × 2048 | 86.4% | **97.3%** | **+10.9pp** | Reg-tiled dominates for N = 512–8192. Compiled wins at N >= 32768 (register spilling). **3.2 Shared memory cache with TMA** (constant ~22 registers, no performance cliff at large N): | Shape (M × N) | Baseline | TMA-smem | Improvement | |----------------|----------|----------|-------------| | 32768 × 4096 | 63.8% | **89.1%** | **+25.3pp** | | 16384 × 8192 | 76.6% | **88.2%** | **+11.6pp** | | 32768 × 8192 | 80.2% | **90.7%** | **+10.5pp** | | 32768 × 32768 | 83.3% | **87.3%** | **+4.0pp** | | 16384 × 16384 | 90.8% | 88.1% | -2.7pp | Hi @shunting314 and @eellison, what do you think about this proposal? cc @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo
comments_excerpt: To resolve this, we can integrate the heuristic routing directly into Inductor's scheduler and update the Triton lowering for the register-tiled path. 1. Scheduler Heuristic We can route the kernels based on the reduction dimension (N), using the crossover point observed in the data. Python import torch from torch._inductor.utils import has_tma_support def get_rmsnorm_strategy(M: int, N: int, dtype: torch.dtype): if N <= 1024: return "standard_persistent" if N <= 8192: return "reg_tiled_fp16_cache" if N > 8192 and has_tma_support(): return "tma_smem_cache" return "multi_pass_reduction" 2. Triton Lowering (Register Tiled Path) For the reg_tiled_fp16_cache, here is the generator logic to dynamically unroll loads and handle the on-the-fly fp32 casting: Python def generate_reg_tiled_rmsnorm(V, N, unroll_factor=2): lines = [] lines.append(f"offs = tl.arange(0, {V.sym_tile})[None, :]") for i in range(unroll_factor): offset_str = f" + {i} * {V.sym_tile}" if i > 0 else "" lines.append(f"x{i} = tl.load(base + offs{offset_str}, mask=mask, other=0.0)") lines.append("ss = tl.zeros([1, TILE], dtype=tl.float32)") for i in range(unroll_factor): lines.append(f"ss += x{i}.to(tl.float32) * x{i}.to(tl.float32)") lines.append(f"inv_rms = tl.rsqrt(tl.sum(ss, axis=1)[:, None] / ({unroll_factor} * TILE) + EPS)") for i in range(unroll_factor): offset_str = f" + {i} * {V.sym_tile}" if i > 0 else "" lines.append(f"w{i} = tl.load(w_ptr + offs{offset_str})") lines.append(f"tl.store(ybase + offs{offset_str}, (x{i}.to(tl.float32) * inv_rms * w{i}).to({V.out_dtype}), mask=mask)") return "\n".join(lines) Resolution Implemented the dual-path optimization for persistent reductions. N <= 8192 routes to the fp16 register-tiled kernel for higher ILP, and N > 8192 routes to the TMA-smem kernel to bypass register pressure. Closing this issue. title: torch.compile: autograd.Function.apply with aliased inputs drops per-slot gradient contributions

issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug When the same Tensor is passed to two (or more) positional tensor arguments of a `torch.autograd.Function.apply(...)`, and the backward returns different values for those positions (e.g. `None` for one slot and a tensor for another), `torch.compile` produces a graph that drops one of the per-slot gradient contributions. In eager, autograd accumulates both slot contributions into a single `.grad` on the shared input. Under `torch.compile`, dynamo collapses the aliased inputs to a single HOP argument and then maps backward returns incorrectly — only one of the duplicated slots' return values ends up as the gradient for the deduped input. cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @amjames @Lucaskabela @jataylo @azahed98 @ydwu4 @bdhirsh @bobrenjc93 @anijain2305 @xmfan — related to the area you worked on in #180642 / #180670 / #180921, but the mechanism here is input aliasing rather than fwd side-effects, and it survives those fixes on current `main`. ### Minimal repro (~50 LOC, pure PyTorch, no triton, no custom ops) ```python import torch class MyFn(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, q, k, v, mask_v_grad: bool): ctx.save_for_backward(q, k, v) ctx.mask_v_grad = mask_v_grad return q * (k + v) @staticmethod def backward(ctx, dout): q, k, v = ctx.saved_tensors dq = dout * (k + v) dk = dout * q dv = dout * q if ctx.mask_v_grad: dk = dk + dv # bwd pre-aggregates; title: Return a view from tensor(requires_grad=False) in autograd function may cause incorrect requires_grad attribute.
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ```python import torch a = torch.rand(4, requires_grad=True) b = a.view(4) assert b.requires_grad and b._is_view() with torch.no_grad(): c = b.view(4) assert c.requires_grad class View(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, x): # return x.data.view(x.shape) return x.detach().view(x.shape) @staticmethod def backward(ctx, grad): return grad d = View.apply(a) assert d.requires_grad and d._is_view() with torch.no_grad(): e = d.view(4) assert e.requires_grad # AssertionError ``` The variable `d` in the `forward` method of other `autograd.Function` implementations may behave differently compared to `b`. If you want to detach from the autograd graph, you can use `.detach()` But within a custom Function forward, since autograd is already disabled, you can just do return `x.view(x.shape)` @albanD Using `.detach()` can also reproduce this issue, while `x.view(x.shape)` seems to resolve it. I think the underlying mechanism might be that: if an autograd function returns a view tensor, subsequent operations performed in a `no_grad` context / `autograd.Function.forward` will inherit the `requires_grad` attribute from the original tensor. This can lead to unexpected behavior during gradient propagation. Why would you expect `e` to require gradients here given that it was created in no_grad mode? And so the output of the custom Function is not considered a view of its input. Leading to slightly different handling downstream. > Why would you expect `e` to require gradients here given that it was created in no_grad mode? In this implementation, the decision to retain activations relies on the requires_grad propagation introduced by the view operation in no_grad mode.

title: Initial benchmarking of jax on some simple kernels
issue_body_excerpt: I've setup a standard system for comparing various jax JIT backends to hand-written CUDA code. The system is a 3000 particle system, and we're evaluating a fused electrostatic + van Der waals repulsion force. Performance aside, I've also noticed fairly severe numerical precision issues in the 32bit backends. That is, comparing the errors between (jax 64 bit vs custom 32 bit) and errors between (jax 32bit vs custom 32 bit), the errors are about 10-50x larger. We've had to increase the error tolerance from 5e-5 to 5e-3 to make the 32bit tests pass. These are the timings for 64/32 bit respectively on a Titan V running on a 12 core Xeon(R) Gold 5118 CPU @ 2.30GHz with 24 threads with CUDA 10.2, jax versions: ``` jax==0.1.70 jaxlib @ https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/cuda102/jaxlib-0.1.47-cp36-none-linux_x86_64.whl ``` ``` precision <class 'numpy.float64'> (64bit vs 64bit) custom force time: 0.0011749029159545898 custom force jvp time: 0.0010498356819152832 testing jit backend: None jax time: 0.11883214712142945 jax jvp time: 0.26240644216537473 testing jit backend: cpu jax time: 0.16196052312850953 jax jvp time: 0.025484113693237304 testing jit backend: gpu jax time: 0.016477890014648437 jax jvp time: 0.02622458219528198 ``` ``` precision <class 'numpy.float32'> (32bit vs 32bit) custom force time: 0.0011496829986572265 custom force jvp time: 0.0010490036010742188 testing jit backend: None jax time: 0.11001898527145386 jax jvp time: 0.19739823102951048 testing jit backend: cpu jax time: 0.10118840456008911 jax jvp time: 0.014006998538970947 testing jit backend: gpu jax time: 0.007918131351470948 jax jvp time: 0.01690457820892334 ``` Some additional notes: 1) JIT compilation time has been removed 2) The actual custom force timings are probably 5-10x faster than listed. This is because it incurs the overhead cost of transferring data from GPU to CPU, allocating buffers, etc. But I suspect jax is doing the same. The code is located at: ``` https://github.com/proteneer/timemachine/tree/Benchmarking ``` To build and run benchmark: ``` Build the custom ops by going into timemachine/cpp 1) mkdir build 2) cd build 3) cmake ../ 4) make -j4 install (this will be installed into a subdirectory of the root folder) Run the benchmarks with: pytest -xsv timemachine/cpp/tests/benchmark.py But be sure to set the right level of precision via the import (config.update("jax_enable_x64", True/False)), and the correct custom force precision. ```

title: Runtime integer calculation overflow
issue_body_excerpt: Not sure if this can be classified as a bug but I thought I would post this just incase it isn't known about. Values known at compile time, and are thus computed in Python, use Python's long int and can represent values outside the range of a normal integer so you can get results that don't quite match. ``` from numba import cuda import numpy as np @cuda.jit def test_kernel(a,b,c,test): i = cuda.grid(1) test[0] = a**b%c test[1] = 11**19%1009 a, b, c = 11, 19, 1009 test = cuda.device_array(2, dtype = np.uint32) test_kernel[1, 1](a,b,c,test) print(a**b%c,test.copy_to_host()) >>> 902 [759 902] ```
comments_excerpt: @uchytilc thank you for submitting this. Is this CUDA specific, or will CPU based functions exhibit the same behaviour? Suspect it's because the cpython bytecode compiler is constant folding and the run time values are out of int range? ```python from numba import njit @njit def demo(a,b,c): print(a**b % c) print(11**19 % 1009) a, b, c = 11, 19, 1009 demo(a,b,c) import dis print(dis.dis(demo)) ``` @stuartarchibald ya I believe that's the problem. If you lower the exponent to where you get a number that is representable within an int the results match. Note from numba meeting: - source of problem is `a**b` invoking an integer exponential and causing undetected overflow. - there's concern that on GPUs that overflow check can be too expensive.

title: pointer should use int64 as its latent operating data type by default to avoid overflow
issue_body_excerpt: ### Describe the bug Its common to do offsetting on pointers for a block of elements, e.g. loading / storing. However, Triton doesn't use int64 as the latent data format for pointers, which leads to overflow in offsetting those pointers, and resulting in illegal memory access. For example, ```python @triton.autotune( configs=[ triton.Config({ "BLOCK_SIZE_M": 128, "BLOCK_SIZE_N": 256, }, num_stages=3, num_warps=8) ], key=["num_rows", "num_cols"] ) @triton.jit def kernel_1(pointer, stride_m, stride_n, num_rows: int, num_cols: int, BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr): pid = tl.program_id(0) num_pid_m = tl.cdiv(num_rows, BLOCK_SIZE_M) pid_m = pid % num_pid_m pid_n = pid // num_pid_m offs_m = pid_m * BLOCK_SIZE_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_M) offs_n = pid_n * BLOCK_SIZE_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N) values = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_N), dtype=tl.float32) pointers = pointer + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n mask = (offs_m[:, None] < num_rows) & (offs_n[None, :] < num_cols) tl.store(pointers, values, mask=mask) ``` This kernel assumes stride_m and stride_n to be int32, and there is no upcasting in `pointers = pointer + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n`, resulting in wrong pointer offsetting for illegal memory access. If we manually upcast the `stride_m` and `stride_n` to int64 first, then `pointers = pointer + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n` will also be upcast implicitly, obtaining correct offsetting. ```python @triton.autotune( configs=[ triton.Config({ "BLOCK_SIZE_M": 128, "BLOCK_SIZE_N": 256, }, num_stages=3, num_warps=8) ], key=["num_rows", "num_cols"] ) @triton.jit def kernel_2(pointer, stride_m: tl.int64, stride_n: tl.int64, num_rows: int, num_cols: int, BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr): pid = tl.program_id(0) num_pid_m = tl.cdiv(num_rows, BLOCK_SIZE_M) pid_m = pid % num_pid_m pid_n = pid // num_pid_m offs_m = pid_m * BLOCK_SIZE_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_M) offs_n = pid_n * BLOCK_SIZE_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N) values = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_N), dtype=tl.float32) pointers = pointer + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n mask = (offs_m[:, None] < num_rows) & (offs_n[None, :] < num_cols) tl.store(pointers, values, mask=mask) ``` To achieve the same offsetting effect akin to other languages, like C++, the pointer should use int64 as the latent data type, automatically upcast when doing offsetting. To reproduce this issue, execute this mini-demo: ```python import torch import triton import triton.language as tl @triton.autotune( configs=[ triton.Config({ "BLOCK_SIZE_M": 128, "BLOCK_SIZE_N": 256, }, num_stages=3, num_warps=8) ], key=["num_rows", "num_cols"] ) @triton.jit def kernel_1(pointer, stride_m, stride_n, num_rows: int, num_cols: int, BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr): pid = tl.program_id(0) num_pid_m = tl.cdiv(num_rows, BLOCK_SIZE_M) pid_m = pid % num_pid_m pid_n = pid // num_pid_m offs_m = pid_m * BLOCK_SIZE_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_M) offs_n = pid_n * BLOCK_SIZE_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N) values = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_N), dtype=tl.float32) pointers = pointer + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n mask = (offs_m[:, None] < num_rows) & (offs_n[None, :] < num_cols) tl.store(pointers, values, mask=mask) @triton.autotune( configs=[ triton.Config({ "BLOCK_SIZE_M": 128, "BLOCK_SIZE_N": 256, }, num_stages=3, num_warps=8) ], key=["num_rows", "num_cols"] ) @triton.jit def kernel_2(pointer, stride_m: tl.int64, stride_n: tl.int64, num_rows: int, num_cols: int, BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr): pid = tl.program_id(0) num_pid_m = tl.cdiv(num_rows, BLOCK_SIZE_M) pid_m = pid % num_pid_m pid_n = pid // num_pid_m offs_m = pid_m * BLOCK_SIZE_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_M) offs_n = pid_n * BLOCK_SIZE_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N) values = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_N), dtype=tl.float32) pointers = pointer + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n mask = (offs_m[:, None] < num_rows) & (offs_n[None, :] < num_cols) tl.store(pointers, values, mask=mask) def main(): num_rows = 46605 num_cols = 152064 tensor = torch.empty((num_rows, num_cols), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16).contiguous() assert tensor.is_contiguous() def grid(meta): return (triton.cdiv(num_rows, meta["BLOCK_SIZE_M"]) * triton.cdiv(num_cols, meta["BLOCK_SIZE_N"]),) torch.cuda.synchronize() # kernel_1[grid](tensor, tensor.stride(0), tensor.stride(1), # num_rows, num_cols) kernel_2[grid](tensor, tensor.stride(0), tensor.stride(1), num_rows, num_cols) torch.cuda.synchronize() if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` ### Environment details Triton: 3.0.0 GPU: H100
comments_excerpt: ```python pointers = pointer + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n ``` The pointer addition does happen in 64-bit, but the overflow happens before that when you multiply the offset by the stride. That means it's your responsibility to upcast the strides to 64-bit if you need the extra range. Closing as not a bug. Then there is another bug. If you manually set the offsetting value to be a integral literal, the resulting pointer is still wrong. For example, let `offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n = 2257846272`, equivalent to `pointers = pointer + 2257846272`. But this syntax will result in wrong pointer, which means triton doesn't handle that integral literal correctly, not like python (handled in 64-bit), nor C++ (handled in 32-bit). Works fine for me: ```python In [4]: import triton ...: import triton.language as tl ...: import torch ...: ...: big = 2257846272 ...: a = torch.empty(big + 1, dtype=torch.int64, device="cuda") ...: ...: @triton.jit ...: def kernel(ptr): ...: tl.store(ptr + 2257846272, 0xdeadbeef) ...: ...: kernel[(1,)](a) ...: print(f'{a[big].item():x}') deadbeef ```

When JAX encounters a Python integer, it is always interpreted as a signed integer of the default width (32 bit or 64 bit, depending on the [X64 flag state](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/default_dtypes.html)). At one time we did have value-dependent dtype semantics, such that integers in the range `(int64.max, uint64.max]` would trigger compilation & tracing for uint64 dtypes, but this often led to unexpected JIT cache misses and brittle code (this is especially true when it comes to NumPy's curious choice of implicitly promoting `int64` and `uint64` to `float64` – it meant that if you passed too large an integer value to otherwise working code, your code might start generating floats instead of ints, which can really cause problems!). title: sum and np.sum() algorithm needs to catch up to improved upstream precision
issue_body_excerpt: This is a "narrative" type of bug report, aka "search the code and compare". No test cases are provided here. Python and NumPy has each changed their `sum()` implementations beyond ordinary linear summation. Specifically: * In https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/100425 (and linked, merged PRs), Python moves to a Neumaier algorithm over the previous naive summation. The slowdown was only 20%, which is probably because all the iterator stuff was taking most of the time... * In the above CPython issue it was mentioned that NumPy does a partial pairwise summation. This provides an improvement of precision in the average case for basically free. (A difference in order was previously noticed in https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/9819#issuecomment-2508969906.) ### Implementation considerations Neumaier is very serial because it has a loop-carried dependency. This can be ameliorated by computing partial sums, which also lends nicely to SIMD. That would introduce some difficulty in numeric reproduction *if* the lane count is dynamically determined. Doing it over the same lane count should always result in the same sequence of operations and be perfectly reproducible. Still, any performant choice (i.e. not 1) would produce results different from upstream. Pairwise is quite amenable to parallelization, from multi-node to multi-core to SIMD. There is again a possible reproducibility issue if the order of operations is determined at runtime. I do not want to think about the CUDA backend. ### Discussion For summation methods there are a lot of small decisions that can affect reproducibility. But, like, is that even a goal? The upstream has no qualms about changing how it sums. I don't think numba should care either. So long as the big-O error bounds for the average and worst cases are on the same order as the upstream, it should be happy about it. Reassociation should be permitted so long as it maintains the bounds (e.g. in pairwise, in SIMD reductions). Oh also. There's not just "the upstream" because np upstream also uses different orders for different backends. https://arxiv.org/html/2411.00442v1 has some pretty pictures. ... And for what is worth, if Neumaier is chosen to implement the builtin `sum()`, I'd still like a way to get something faster like pairwise.

title: [Inductor] Filter extremely bad triton configs by device information for triton heuristics
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch The current workflow for the triton heuristics is to generate a series of triton configs and then run autotune to a best config. Usually these config generated are based on well known practices, and at the same time try to cover as many cases as possible because autotune is a onetime effort and it doesn't seem to hurt much to evaluate more configs. With max_autotune, it also tend to add or keep more configs to bench. This workflow is simple and straight forward. But we saw the config included lacks the consideration of the device capabilities such as the number CTAs especially when the GPU in the market becomes more diverse: low end GPU may have a few CTAs per GPU, while high end GPU have hundreds. For example, for the following case: ``` import torch import time start_time = time.perf_counter() class TestModule(torch.nn.Module): # Input tensors that are generated randomly def __init__(self, sel_device, training): torch.manual_seed(777) super(TestModule, self).__init__() self.inp = torch.empty_strided(size=[16, 4096, 1024], stride=[4194304, 1024, 1], dtype=torch.bfloat16, device='cpu').uniform_(-1, 1).to(device=sel_device).requires_grad_(training) def forward(self): r = torch.sum(self.inp, [0], False) # traced line: 1010 return r device = "xpu" m = TestModule(device, False) m = torch.compile(m) out = m() out = out.to("cpu") end_time = time.perf_counter() print("Total time:", str(end_time - start_time)) ``` Inductor persistent_reduction will generate and auto tune 4 XBLOCK configurations with the reduction size = 16: ``` 1. {'XBLOCK': 1} 2. {'XBLOCK': 8} 3. {'XBLOCK': 32} 4. {'XBLOCK': 128} ``` These will bench 4 grid configurations: ``` 1. {'XBLOCK': 1} -> grid (4194304, 1, 1) 2. {'XBLOCK': 8} -> grid (524288, 1, 1) 3. {'XBLOCK': 32} -> grid (131072, 1, 1) 4. {'XBLOCK': 128} -> grid (32768, 1, 1) ``` Extreme cases like 4194304 thread blocks /work groups with reduction on 16 elements is obviously bad and will mostly perform the worst. We will spend much of the time benchmarking some very bad config without a chance to win. What's more, when we running this config in weak GPU or in a simulator, this kind of extreme case will take much of the time and make the benchmark time unacceptable. One method to deal with this is to avoid including such a config at the beginning by applying the knowledge of the problem size and the device capabilities. But this will make the config logic too complex and dynamic considering we already have a lot of cases to handle for pointwise, reduction, persistent reduction and so on. The existing way doing limited check and adding configs is still ideal for simplicity. The suggest approach is to simply add the capability to perform a scrub process which filter out the extreme triton config by device information after all configs are created. This makes the logic of filtering centralized and not intrusive for the config generation logic. And this filtering config by device information can be controlled by a flag so that user can turn on or off. @ezyang @EikanWang ### Alternatives _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_
comments_excerpt: For configurations that do not make sense from a performance perspective, we should exclude them from the search space. The key point is how to evaluate the performance impact of configurations in an efficient way. @jerrychenhf , are you proposing adding new device-capabilities-aware filters to filter out configurations? Say - Step 1: Keep the current configuration logic to produce configurations - Step 2: Apply filters to the produced configurations for performance Is my understanding correct? @EikanWang > are you proposing adding new device-capabilities-aware filters to filter out configurations? Yes > * Step 1: Keep the current configuration logic to produce configurations > * Step 2: Apply filters to the produced configurations for performance Step 1: Exactly yes. Step 2: Apply filters to reduce "OBVIOUS BAD" config based on device capabilities, grid and per cta work information. Will NOT try to figure out new config which might be more performant than the current ones. Figuring out and add more config will be always part of Step 1. Step 1: focus to getting enough configs to autotune. It may have two types of configs: **A**. General configs added only considering the type of kernel like pointwise, reduction, etc **B**. More performant configs added by considering the problem shape, device capabilities, etc Step 2: do a reduce of configs based on some simple principles regarding the device capabilities, grid and per cta work information. This is major for simplify the Step 1 - **A** type of configs since we can add generally more configs without very careful checking. So even we have Step 2 (remove known worst configs waste time to benchmark). It is still valuable in Step 1 to add **B** type of configs (figure to include best configs in search space).

title: [BUG] cudf-polars streaming-mode broadcast bug
issue_body_excerpt: Claude-generated description of the issue and repro: ``` """Minimal repro: cudf-polars streaming-mode broadcast bug for `with_columns(pl.lit(<numpy_array>))` at >~1M rows. Setup: polars==1.38.1, cudf==26.04, on NVIDIA L40 / Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.x Symptom: RuntimeError: Cannot broadcast columns of length nrows=N to target_length=N/2 Trigger: A LazyFrame whose `with_columns` adds a literal column built from a Series/numpy array of the same length as the source (i.e. a row-aligned column literal, not a scalar `pl.lit(value)`). At >~1M rows the streaming executor partitions the upstream into halves but does not partition the literal alongside; the subsequent broadcast then sees a full-length column being placed into a half-length partition and raises. Workaround: pl.GPUEngine(executor="in-memory") # skips the streaming code path """ from __future__ import annotations import numpy as np import polars as pl def make_lf(n: int) -> pl.LazyFrame: return pl.LazyFrame({ "key": np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 100, size=n, dtype=np.int32), }).with_columns( pl.lit(np.arange(n, dtype=np.uint64)).alias("var_id"), ) def try_collect(n: int, executor: str) -> str: engine = pl.GPUEngine(raise_on_fail=True, executor=executor) try: df = make_lf(n).collect(engine=engine) return f"OK ({df.height} rows)" except RuntimeError as e: return f"FAIL: {e}" if __name__ == "__main__": print("Polars:", pl.__version__) import cudf print("cudf: ", cudf.__version__) print() for n in [100_000, 500_000, 1_000_000, 1_500_000, 2_000_000, 5_000_000]: print(f"n={n:>10} streaming: {try_collect(n, 'streaming')}") print() print(f"n={5_000_000:>10} in-memory: {try_collect(5_000_000, 'in-memory')}") ```

title: hipBLASLt path ignores backward fp16_alt_impl for Half GEMMs, causing FTZ in backward and silent training divergence on gfx90a

issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug # Summary On AMD gfx90a (MI250X), PyTorch 2.7+ defaults `blasPreferredBackend()` to `Cublaslt` on ROCm. On this path, backward `float16` GEMMs appear to run without the ROCm backward-pass alternative implementation that preserves fp16 subnormals. As a result, subnormal fp16 inputs in backward GEMMs are flushed to zero, which can silently corrupt gradients and cause training divergence. Forcing rocBLAS with: ```python torch.backends.cuda.preferred_blas_library("cublas") ``` restores the expected behavior on the same system. ## Minimal reproducer ```python import torch dtype = torch.float16 M = K = N = 64 sub_val = torch.finfo(dtype).tiny / 2 ref = M * sub_val def check_backward(force_rocblas=False): if force_rocblas: torch.backends.cuda.preferred_blas_library("cublas") print("PyTorch:", torch.__version__) print("ROCm:", torch.version.hip) if hasattr(torch.backends.cuda, "preferred_blas_library"): print("preferred_blas_library:", torch.backends.cuda.preferred_blas_library()) x = torch.ones(M, K, dtype=dtype, device="cuda") w = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.ones(K, N, dtype=dtype, device="cuda")) d = torch.full((M, N), sub_val, dtype=dtype, device="cuda") (x @ w).backward(d) torch.cuda.synchronize() val = w.grad[0, 0].item() print("grad[0,0] =", val, "expected =", ref) print("Default backend") check_backward(force_rocblas=False) print("\nForced rocBLAS") check_backward(force_rocblas=True) ``` ## Observed behavior - PyTorch 2.3.0 + ROCm 6.0: default backend is rocBLAS, backward result matches `ref`. - PyTorch 2.9.1 + ROCm 6.4: default backend is hipBLASLt, backward result is `0.0`. - PyTorch 2.9.1 + ROCm 6.4 with forced rocBLAS: backward result again matches `ref`. With BLAS logging enabled, rocBLAS backward GEMMs are dispatched with `flags 4` (`fp16_alt_impl`), while hipBLASLt forward/backward matmuls look identical apart from transpose, suggesting the backward guard is not wired through the hipBLASLt path. ## Expected behavior One of these should hold: 1. Backward fp16 GEMMs on ROCm should preserve the current rocBLAS behavior when PyTorch selects hipBLASLt by default. 2. If hipBLASLt cannot support the backward-safe path yet, gfx90a should not default to `Cublaslt` for fp16 training workloads where this changes numerical behavior. ## Likely root cause `ROCmBackwardPassGuard` is honored on the rocBLAS path, where PyTorch passes `rocblas_gemm_flags_fp16_alt_impl`, but not on `gemm_internal_cublaslt<at::Half>()`. title: [FEA] Should `Rolling.apply` use pure numba rather than jitify?
issue_body_excerpt: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.** cuDF supports [rolling.apply](https://docs.rapids.ai/api/cudf/latest/user_guide/api_docs/api/cudf.series.rolling/#cudf.Series.rolling) for executing a custom python function over the specified rolling windows. It works by taking a PTX string compiled in python by numba and handing it off to a rolling aggregation with `kind == PTX`, which is then used through `rolling_window`. Ultimately this invokes jitify and a series of parsing and compilation steps leading to the final [kernel](https://github.com/rapidsai/cudf/blob/81bb6f1ea46d633548b9bf534c93a28ba66909ea/cpp/src/rolling/jit/kernel.cu#L45) that computes the result. Historically a similar process served to make APIs like `Series.applymap` work but over time we migrated to an approach that puts together the final kernel in numba rather than c++ for several reasons: - The parsing approach through jitify trips up in several useful cases, such as when numba delivers PTX containing multiple function definitions - The full numba approach allows for extension types to support null values - The full numba approach benefits from features such as LTO through pynvjitlink **Describe the solution you'd like** A pure numba implementation of `Rolling.apply`, possibly with extension type support. For non nullable data, the implementation could look something like this: ```python def count_if_gt_3(window): count = 0 for i in window: if i > 3: count += 1 return count devfunc = cuda.jit(device=True)(count_if_gt_3) out = np.zeros(len(s)) @cuda.jit def kernel(data, win_size, min_periods, out): tid = cuda.grid(1) start = max(0, tid - win_size + 1) end = tid + 1 thread_win = data[start:end] res = devfunc(thread_win) out[tid] = res ``` The above seems to get me the correct result in a few test cases locally, of course the real impl would need more to account for `min_periods`, other dtypes, and more. A _null sensitive_ implementation seems possible as well building on a lot of what we already have. The idea revolves around assembling the data into a `cuda.local.array` of `MaskedType` and then passing that array into the UDF as written. The existing implementations of operations between MaskedTypes should take care of the rest. ```python @cuda.jit def kernel(data, mask, win_size, min_periods, out_data, out_mask): tid = cuda.grid(1) start = max(0, tid - win_size + 1) end = tid + 1 local = cuda.local.array(win_size, Masked(types.int64)) # place this window of data into thread local memory as an array of MaskedTypes for i in range(0, end-start): local[i] = Masked(data[start+i], mask_get(mask, start+i)) # the device function now iterates through the array of MaskedTypes # any operations are resolved through MaskedType's overloads res = devfunc(local) out_data[tid] = res.value out_mask[tid] = res.valid ``` Currently however creating a `cuda.local.array` of extension types needs a few changes (cc @gmarkall). The above would enable handling nulls explicitly within supported UDFs in conditional logic: ```python def count_if_gt_3(window): count = 0 for i in window: if i != cudf.NA: if i > 3: count += 1 else: return -1 return count ``` **Describe alternatives you've considered** One disadvantage of this approach is that we'd need to reimplement logic around handling all of the keyword arguments currently supported for rolling without a custom aggregation, such as `center` and `min_periods`. This would have to be maintained separately from libcudf.

issue_body_excerpt: While the current ability to pass a dict of dtypes to `rtol=` and `atol=` is nice, in practice it is used pretty rarely meaning that double precision routines are often tested with the same precision as single precision ones. This is mostly fine, since correctness errors should still fail, but it gives very little with respect to testing expected higher precision of `double` versions. I think it would be helpful to add a testing mechanism based on `assert_array_almost_equal_nulp`. Or something similar to it, maybe an integer meaning a multiple of the `finfo(...).eps` or so.

title: Matrix multiply incorrect for large tensors
issue_body_excerpt: ### Description I am pushing this [issue](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/issues/1599) upstream; my guess is it will end up being an XLA issue. I will eventually provide a more minimal example than [this example](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/issues/1599#issuecomment-2677089400) that should end up just being a batched matrix multiply, but it may be worthwhile to make this issue now in case this is a known memory issue. Basically, a simple `vmap_chunked` operator that copies the batching in chunks logic in `jax.lax.map` is used to batch a function that performs a matrix multiplication. When the ``chunk_size`` is large, this matrix multiplication is performed incorrectly. The results are both wrong and not deterministic. In [this example](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/issues/1599#issuecomment-2677089400), the issue occurs when `chunk_size=1000`. The issue vanishes when `chunk_size=100`. Perhaps noteworthy is that the program completes faster than should be possible when the issue occurs. For `chunk_size=1000`, the program completes in 10 seconds and for `chunk_size=100` the program takes 15 minutes. If this only occurs on machines when memory limits are being approached, it would be much better if JAX or maybe XLA can ensure that the program fails rather than completing silently. ### System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.) ``` WARNING:2025-02-23 15:25:23,569:jax._src.xla_bridge:969: An NVIDIA GPU may be present on this machine, but a CUDA-enabled jaxlib is not installed. title: [BUG] Decimal division loses precision when dividing by decimals with fractional parts
issue_body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** When performing division on Decimal64Dtype columns in cuDF, the result consistently loses the decimal fraction and becomes zero, depending on the precisions and scales of the input columns. This behavior is incorrect and does not match the expected results when calculated manually. **Steps/Code to reproduce bug** Here is a minimal code sample that reproduces the issue: ``` import cudf from decimal import Decimal # Test cases with varying precisions and scales test_cases = [ {'a_dtype': cudf.Decimal64Dtype(2, 2), 'b_dtype': cudf.Decimal64Dtype(1, 0), 'description': 'Case 1: Dividing by an integer (scale=0)'}, {'a_dtype': cudf.Decimal64Dtype(2, 2), 'b_dtype': cudf.Decimal64Dtype(3, 2), 'description': 'Case 2: Dividing by a decimal-only real number (precision=scale)'}, {'a_dtype': cudf.Decimal64Dtype(3, 2), 'b_dtype': cudf.Decimal64Dtype(3, 2), 'description': 'Case 3: Dividing by a real number with both integer and decimal parts (precision > scale)'}, ] # Loop through the test cases for case in test_cases: print(case['description']) df = cudf.DataFrame({'a': [Decimal('0.02')], 'b': [Decimal('2')]}).astype( { 'a': case['a_dtype'], 'b': case['b_dtype'], } ) df['res'] = df['a'] / df['b'] print(df['res'], df['res'].dtype.precision, df['res'].dtype.scale) ``` Running this script produces the following output: ``` Case 1: Dividing by an integer (scale=0) 0 0.010000 Name: res, dtype: decimal64 6 6 Case 2: Dividing by a decimal-only real number (precision=scale) 0 0.000000 Name: res, dtype: decimal64 8 6 Case 3: Dividing by a real number with both integer and decimal parts (precision > scale) 0 0.000000 Name: res, dtype: decimal64 9 6 ``` **Expected behavior** The division results should retain the decimal fraction regardless of the precisions and scales of the input columns. Specifically: - Case 1 (Dividing by an integer): The result is correct (0.01) as expected. - Case 2 (Dividing by a decimal-only real number): The result is incorrect (0.00), but the expected value is 0.01. - Case 3 (Dividing by a real number with both integer and decimal parts): The result is incorrect (0.00), but the expected value is 0.01. For all cases, the division operation should preserve precision and produce consistent and accurate results based on manual calculations. **Additional context** This issue is consistently reproducible and appears to be related to how cuDF calculates the output precision and scale during division operations involving decimals. The incorrect handling leads to a loss of significant digits in the result.
comments_excerpt: This is expected behavior. Decimals are integers with a piece of scale metadata. Consider the integer value representation that is behind the decimals: Case 1 is computing the result as `2 / 2 = 1` with scale `2 - 0 = 2`. This gives `0.01`. Case 2 is computing the result as `2 / 200 = 0` with scale `2 - 2 = 0`. This gives `0`. Case 3 is computing the result as `2 / 200 = 0` with scale `2 - 2 = 0`. This gives `0`. Truncation is expected when the divisor has a scale that is equal-or-less-than the dividend. You can try scaling up the divisors to have a higher scale (so that the internal representation of the values is `20` or `200` or `2000` instead of `2`) before performing division. The test cases you provided have the least-possible scale that can still express `0.02`. Increasing the scale of the divisor to `cudf.Decimal64Dtype(4, 4)` makes all the test cases pass: ```python df['res'] = df['a'].astype(cudf.Decimal64Dtype(4, 4)) / df['b'] ``` cuDF's default decimal behavior in Python is designed to match SQL, but this doesn't obviate the need for starting with the appropriate scale for computation. libcudf does not upscale inputs pre-emptively: - https://github.com/rapidsai/cudf/blob/79a986067688c18b3d431c7a3acc23e2307fb668/python/cudf/cudf/core/column/decimal.py#L437 - https://github.com/rapidsai/cudf/blob/79a986067688c18b3d431c7a3acc23e2307fb668/python/cudf/cudf/core/column/decimal.py#L458-L459 Are you trying to match another library's behavior? It is usually possible to adapt the cuDF convention to match a different convention. For example, this matches the Arrow conventions (https://arrow.apache.org/docs/cpp/compute.html#arithmetic-functions, scroll down a bit): ```python def match_arrow_division(left, right): """Divide decimal series s1 and s2, matching Arrow's rules for precision and scale.""" s1 = left.dtype.scale s2 = right.dtype.scale p1 = left.dtype.precision p2 = right.dtype.precision out_scale = max(4, s1 + p2 - s2 + 1) out_precision = p1 - s1 + s2 + out_scale print("s1:", s1, "s2:", s2, "p1:", p1, "p2:", p2, "out_scale:", out_scale, "out_precision:", out_precision) result = left.astype(cudf.Decimal64Dtype(out_precision, out_scale + s2 - s1)) / right return result.astype(cudf.Decimal64Dtype(out_precision, out_scale)) ``` Output: ``` Case 1: Dividing by an integer (scale=0) s1: 2 s2: 0 p1: 2 p2: 1 out_scale: 4 out_precision: 4 cuDF: 0.0100 decimal64 4 4 Arrow: 0.0100 decimal128(4, 4) Case 2: Dividing by a decimal-only real number (precision=scale) s1: 2 s2: 2 p1: 2 p2: 3 out_scale: 4 out_precision: 6 cuDF: 0.0100 decimal64 6 4 Arrow: 0.0100 decimal128(6, 4) Case 3: Dividing by a real number with both integer and decimal parts (precision > scale) s1: 2 s2: 2 p1: 3 p2: 3 out_scale: 4 out_precision: 7 cuDF: 0.0100 decimal64 7 4 Arrow: 0.0100 decimal128(7, 4) /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/cudf/core/column/decimal.py:80: UserWarning: cuDF truncates when downcasting decimals to a lower scale. title: [inductor][static launcher] Missing runtime dtype validation for pointer-typed Triton args can silently produce incorrect results
issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug I believe there is a missing runtime validation in the static Triton launcher path for pointer-typed Triton kernel arguments. I reproduced this on a pip-installed `torch==2.8.0` environment (not running from a source checkout). In that version, the relevant file on the executed code path is: - `torch/_inductor/runtime/static_cuda_launcher.py` I also inspected current `main`, where this code has been renamed to `torch/_inductor/runtime/static_triton_launcher.py`, and I did not find an equivalent runtime validation for pointer-typed tensor dtypes there either. ## Summary The static launcher appears to compress all pointer-typed Triton arguments to `"O"` and does not preserve or validate the original pointer element dtype (for example `*fp16`, `*bf16`, `*fp32`) before launch. This means a kernel compiled assuming one pointer dtype can still be launched at runtime with a tensor of a different dtype, without a clear validation error. The failure mode is not a clean Python exception. Instead, the kernel launches successfully and produces silent incorrect numerics. ## Why this looks unsafe In the static launcher path: - pointer-typed Triton args are compressed to `"O"` - the compressed launcher signature is used for launch - the launcher only sees a pointer-like Python object and extracts its device pointer As a result, the launch path does not appear to validate that the runtime tensor dtype still matches the Triton pointer type used during compilation. ## Minimal reproducer This reproducer does **not** require a statically launched user-defined Triton kernel. A wrong fake/meta dtype on a custom op is enough to cause a downstream Inductor-generated Triton pointwise kernel to be compiled for one dtype and then launched with a runtime tensor of another dtype. ```python import os os.environ.setdefault("TORCHINDUCTOR_STRICT_STATIC_CUDA_LAUNCHER", "1") import torch @torch.library.custom_op("custom_ops::bad_meta_mul", mutates_args=()) def bad_meta_mul(a: torch.Tensor, b: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Runtime implementation returns float32 return a * b @bad_meta_mul.register_fake def bad_meta_mul_fake(a, b): # Intentionally wrong fake/meta dtype return torch.empty_like(a, dtype=torch.bfloat16) @torch.compile(fullgraph=True, options={"fx_graph_cache": False}) def f(a, b): x = torch.ops.custom_ops.bad_meta_mul(a, b) return x + 1 torch.manual_seed(0) a = torch.randn(1 << 20, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) b = torch.randn(1 << 20, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) ref = torch.ops.custom_ops.bad_meta_mul(a, b) + 1 out = f(a, b) torch.cuda.synchronize() diff = (out.float() - ref.float()).abs() print("out.dtype:", out.dtype) print("ref.dtype:", ref.dtype) print("allclose:", torch.allclose(out.float(), ref.float(), atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4)) print("max_abs_err:", diff.max().item()) print("mean_abs_err:", diff.mean().item()) print("out[:8]:", out[:8].cpu()) print("ref[:8]:", ref[:8].cpu()) ``` ## Observed behavior On my setup, this does not fail fast. It launches and produces incorrect results. Observed output: ``` out.dtype: torch.float32 ref.dtype: torch.float32 allclose: False max_abs_err: 1.0000004768371582 mean_abs_err: 0.5015609264373779 ``` I also ran a control experiment with the same setup but a correct fake registration (dtype=torch.float32). In that case: ``` allclose: True max_abs_err: 0.0 ``` ## Additional launcher instrumentation I locally instrumented the static launcher and observed: - `use_static_cuda_launcher: True` - `static_launch_user_defined_triton_kernels: False` and the following launch-time evidence: ``` [static-launcher] signature: {'in_out_ptr0': '*bf16', 'xnumel': 'i32'} compressed_arg_tys: Oi [static-launcher] launch: {'kernel': 'triton_poi_fused_add_0', 'arg_tys': 'Oi', 'runtime_args': ['Tensor(dtype=torch.float32, shape=(1048576,), device=cuda:0)', '1048576']} ``` So the compile-time Triton pointer type was *bf16, but the actual runtime tensor passed through the static launcher was torch.float32, and the kernel still launched instead of raising a validation error. ## Expected behavior If the Triton pointer signature expected at compile time does not match the runtime tensor dtype, the launcher should fail fast with a clear error. Even if the root cause is ultimately a bad fake/meta implementation, the current behavior seems unsafe because it can silently produce wrong results instead of failing fast. ## Possible fix direction One possible fix would be to preserve the original Triton arg types for non-constexpr arguments in the static launcher path, and validate pointer-typed tensor dtypes before calling _launch_kernel. For example: - keep the original Triton arg types alongside the compressed launcher signature - for pointer args, compare the runtime tensor dtype against the expected pointer element dtype - raise a clear error on mismatch instead of launching ### Error logs ```text There is no clear Python exception in the failing case. title: Triton int64 overflow bug
issue_body_excerpt: To compute `(a * b) % c`, if `a * b` is greater than `max(int32_t)`, then the final result is incorrect. Reproducer: https://github.com/Jokeren/triton-samples/blob/main/int64-mod.py
comments_excerpt: You are right. I am aware of this problem -- just need to come up with a proper fix that doesn't affect performance (int64 are expensive on GPUs). Right now Triton directly translate to `llvm.mul`, which uses the 2-complements and overflows. Casting inputs to a bigger int type before multiplying is the way to do it but my incur some overhead. I have started working on a fix, which includes specializing kernels so that `get_program_id(dim)` returns int16 on small grids, which would remove the performance overhead in most cases that matter :) Found a workaround. title: [FEA] libcudf implementation of "intuitive" decimal division
issue_body_excerpt: The `libcudf` implementation of decimal division is really fixed-point division, and does not behave intuitively compared with the accepted conventions in (say) the SQL world. For example, dividing `DECIMAL64(200,-2)` by `DECIMAL64(300,-2)` (which is equivalent to `2.00 / 3.00`) gives a result of `DECIMAL64(0,0)` due to the implementation of `fixed_point<>::operator/()` which simply divides the internal integer values and sets the output scale to the input scale difference. This is not useful in a an SQL context, where the intuitive result would be something like `DECIMAL64(66,-2)` (i.e. `0.66`). While the intuitively-correct behavior *is* achievable using standard `libcudf` operators, for example by pre-scaling the numerator to account for the denominator scale, the required operator graph translation is therefore not 1:1. This has been reported before in this repo, most recently in cuDF issue #17448. For the Velox (and Presto) GPU projects, it was decided to write custom kernels to perform decimal division, in order to achieve the desired behavior in a single operator, although the use of that custom operator is of course limited to "function mode" (i.e. as an alternative to `cudf::binary_operation(X, Y, cudf::binary_operator::DIV)`) and cannot be used by cudf AST mode. These kernels are in Velox PR 16750. Additional custom kernels were implemented to support Presto GPU aggregations (most obviously `AVG`) which require a division of a sum value with specific handling of any overflow. These are currently contained in Velox PR 16751. For various reasons, it is not ideal that custom CUDA kernels exist in the Velox source code repo, and so while they will be tolerated for the initial implementation of GPU Decimal, the long-term expectation is that they be moved to the cuDF repo, perhaps as the start of end-product-specific code. While specific to Velox/Presto at first, it is likely that other SQL (and probably non-SQL) implementations will require the same behavior, so ideally the implementation should be general enough, or able to be generalized later as additional applications arise.

Thanks @bdice for continuing the discussion. It seems like @a-hirota's contribution in https://github.com/rapidsai/cudf/pull/19861 is adding a free function for a more flexible decimal divide. @simoneves Would this implementation serve the Presto-Velox use case?

title: [QST] [Performance in pylibcudf with stream] Unexpected GIL ThreadSync and CUDASync in pylibcudf Parquet Reading
issue_body_excerpt: Dear pylibcudf Team, I'm writing to share my findings from my ongoing study on pipelining Parquet reading as setup details in #18278. I'm really excited about the new feature that enables the use of streams in pylibcudf. I've conducted tests with this new feature and it successfully creates a pipeline similar to that in libcudf in most of my test cases. Thanks for this feature! However, when I perform small-granularity and short-running reads where each `read_parquet` operation has a runtime of less than 10 ms, I've noticed that the pipeline is gone, `read_parquet` operations from different threads/streams seem to interfere with each other. I investigated this issue using nsys and discovered two unnecessary synchronization points: one from CUDA synchronization and another from the GIL thread synchronization. I've tried a few workarounds, but I haven't been able to eliminate these problems and overheads. # GIL thread sync ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/76c54d07-2dd2-4fe3-a5fd-e98c0bd2ed46) ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f28fb05c-3c6e-44d9-ab51-4206c914b7b2) In this thread, there is a gap time between two `read_parquet` calls, due to a `pthread_cond_timedwait` from GIL. # CUDA sync ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/848df7de-ee48-47da-9778-76eeafa044b0) ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f4d2ac05-bae5-4416-8465-8ad714936186) At the same time, another thread also has an gap time, but due to `cudaStreamSynchronize`, which is called inside of the cpython. As you see, these two factors happening at the same time breaks the building of a pipeline and the performance, as I could do in libcudf.

title: Understanding Triton GEMM FP8 performance
issue_body_excerpt: Hello, we have measured the FP8 GEMM performance using Triton on NVIDIA H100 (500 W, 1980 MHz). We would like to request your help in understanding if the performance is expected. Since H100 FP8 only supports NT GEMM (matrix B is transposed), so we tested the performance with matrix B transposed and not transposed. We also tested with `fp8_fast_accum=True` and `fp8_fast_accum=False`. Results overview: - Comparing to the CUBLAS performance, the performance of Triton GEMM is ~15% lower than the CUBLAS GEMM performance - `fp8_fast_accum = True` has a significant positive impact on the performance. ![triton_vs_cublas_fp8_h1002](https://github.com/openai/triton/assets/17482891/f567e9ba-1ee0-4120-8251-3a1094264b68) Our benchmark: [fp8_matmul.py.zip](https://github.com/openai/triton/files/13034506/fp8_matmul.py.zip) Questions: - Are the performance numbers expected? - What does `fp8_fast_accum=True` do? Does it set `CUBLASLT_MATMUL_DESC_FAST_ACCUM=1` and/or do something differently? Thank you very much!

title: RFC: Separate NumPy and CPython implementions/functionality.
issue_body_excerpt: This is an RFC on altering Numba's fundamental numerical functionality to better reflect what is present in Python/NumPy. The intended impact of this is to: * Ensure better reproducibility, i.e. Numba will more closely follow what would happen in the interpreter. * Alter performance characteristics with an anticipated net performance gain. * Create conceptually easier paths to follow to achieve higher performance. **Current state:** At present, the Numba code base implements a large number of the functions found in Python builtins, Python's `operator`, `math` and `cmath` modules, and NumPy. Due to historical reasons (largely from the way in which the compiler was bootstrapped) a lot of the implementations of the functions are reasonable approximations for "common" input values that are in use by most users, but they often fail to replicate functionality _exactly_. This "reasonable approximation" has served Numba well, but the current state has a few fundamental problems: 1. The functions often call into each others' implementations, for example NumPy `ufuncs` that "borrow" implementation details from the `math` module. The performance characteristics can be somewhat unpredictable due to this as the implementations from Python modules often contain exception handling whereas NumPy does not. Exceptions lead to branches which lead to lost optimisation opportunities in e.g. vectorization. 2. The implementations are sufficiently acceptable along "common" paths, but are often not correctly implemented with respect to things like type promotion or error handling. 3. Whilst this is an implementation detail, due to the state of the current code base the reusability of the implementations across hardware targets involves a lot of boilerplate and copy-paste to fix things e.g. on CUDA swapping libm/intrinsic `cos` calls for CUDA libdevice `cos` calls. 4. Numba's type system aliases Python `int` with NumPy `intp`, `float` with NumPy `float64` and `complex` with NumPy `complex128`. This makes it hard to be specific about what the behaviour _should_ be when e.g. raw numerical values interact with e.g. NumPy functions. **Some examples of the above issues:** This example demonstrates the problems noted in 2. that for simple integer and float inputs to a "power"-like function quite a large spectrum of result values, result types and error handling behaviours are produced. ```python import operator import math import numpy as np def operator_pow(a, b): return operator.pow(a, b) def math_pow(a, b): return math.pow(a, b) def np_pow(a, b): return np.power(a, b) for x, y in ((2, 2), (2.1, 2), (2.1, 1.3), (2.1, 0.3), (2, 0.3), (2.1, -1), (2, -1), (2.1, -1.2), (-2., -1), (-2, -2.1), (-2.1, -0.2)): buf = [f"x={x:<4}, y={y:<4}: "] for key, fn in (('o', operator_pow), ('m', math_pow), ('n', np_pow)): try: o = fn(x, y) if isinstance(o, (int, np.integer)): prec = '6' else: prec = '6.4' ofmt = f'{key}: {str(type(o)):<18}{o:<{prec}} ' except Exception as e: ofmt = f'{key}: {e} ' buf.append(ofmt) print(''.join(buf)) ``` which produces: ``` x=2 , y=2 : o: <class 'int'> 4 m: <class 'float'> 4.0 n: <class 'numpy.int64'>4 x=2.1 , y=2 : o: <class 'float'> 4.41 m: <class 'float'> 4.41 n: <class 'numpy.float64'>4.41 x=2.1 , y=1.3 : o: <class 'float'> 2.624 m: <class 'float'> 2.624 n: <class 'numpy.float64'>2.624 x=2.1 , y=0.3 : o: <class 'float'> 1.249 m: <class 'float'> 1.249 n: <class 'numpy.float64'>1.249 x=2 , y=0.3 : o: <class 'float'> 1.231 m: <class 'float'> 1.231 n: <class 'numpy.float64'>1.231 x=2.1 , y=-1 : o: <class 'float'> 0.4762 m: <class 'float'> 0.4762 n: <class 'numpy.float64'>0.4762 x=2 , y=-1 : o: <class 'float'> 0.5 m: <class 'float'> 0.5 n: Integers to negative integer powers are not allowed. x=2.1 , y=-1.2: o: <class 'float'> 0.4105 m: <class 'float'> 0.4105 n: <class 'numpy.float64'>0.4105 x=-2.0, y=-1 : o: <class 'float'> -0.5 m: <class 'float'> -0.5 n: <class 'numpy.float64'>-0.5 x=-2 , y=-2.1: o: <class I applied a Conv block with 2 features with (2,2) kernel size, no bias, "same" padding, (1,1) strides to a (1,4,4,1) array both in flax and keras, then calculated flops used for each. Keras flop calculation would return 256 which makes sense (2 kernels * 16 output cells * (4 mul + 4 sum) = 256). If we were to dissect the number 196 by dividing it by 2 kernels and 16 output cells, we would get 6.125 flops per cell. title: [BUG] Unable to write `timedelta64[s]` type correctly with parquet writer
issue_body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** Only when we have `timedelta64[s]` dtype for a column, the parquet writer seems to be writing it as a `timedelta64[ms]` column which is leading both cudf & pyarrow parquet readers to pickup the column type incorrectly. **Steps/Code to reproduce bug** Follow this guide http://matthewrocklin.com/blog/work/2018/02/28/minimal-bug-reports to craft a minimal bug report. This helps us reproduce the issue you're having and resolve the issue more quickly. ```python In [1]: import cudf In [3]: df = cudf.DataFrame({"seconds": cudf.Series([1234, 3456, 32442], dtype='timedelta64[s]')}) In [4]: df Out[4]: seconds 0 0 days 00:20:34 1 0 days 00:57:36 2 0 days 09:00:42 In [5]: df.dtypes Out[5]: seconds timedelta64[s] dtype: object In [6]: df.to_parquet("a") In [7]: cudf.read_parquet("a") Out[7]: seconds 0 0 days 00:20:34 1 0 days 00:57:36 2 0 days 09:00:42 In [8]: cudf.read_parquet("a").dtypes Out[8]: seconds timedelta64[ms] # Should be timedelta64[s] dtype: object In [9]: import pyarrow as pa In [10]: pa.parquet.read_table("a") Out[10]: pyarrow.Table seconds: time32[ms] not null # Should be time32[s] ---- seconds: [[00:20:34.000,00:57:36.000,09:00:42.000]] # If we now try to write & read using pyarrow the dtype stays intact: In [11]: pa_table = df.to_arrow() In [12]: pa_table Out[12]: pyarrow.Table seconds: duration[s] ---- seconds: [[1234,3456,32442]] In [13]: pa.parquet.write_table(pa_table, "a") In [15]: pa.parquet.read_table("a") Out[15]: pyarrow.Table seconds: duration[s] ---- seconds: [[1234,3456,32442]] In [17]: import pandas as pd In [18]: pd.read_parquet("a") Out[18]: seconds 0 0 days 00:20:34 1 0 days 00:57:36 2 0 days 09:00:42 In [19]: pd.read_parquet("a").dtypes Out[19]: seconds timedelta64[ns] dtype: object In [21]: pa.parquet.read_metadata("a").schema Out[21]: <pyarrow._parquet.ParquetSchema object at 0x7fc8e622b0c0> required group field_id=-1 schema { optional int64 field_id=-1 seconds; } ``` **Expected behavior** We are writing all other `timedelta` resolutions(`ns`, `ms`, `us`) correctly. issue_body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug Here is the code to reproduce the bug: ```python import torch torch._inductor.config.fallback_random = True def foo(a): x = a.clone() # this line is necessary to reproduce the error y = x.as_strided((2, 2), (1, 1), 0) y.add_(1.0) return y torch.manual_seed(0) a = torch.randn([2, 2, 10]) a_ = a.clone() res1 = foo(a) res2 = torch.compile(foo, backend='aot_eager')(a_) torch.testing.assert_close(res1, res2, equal_nan=True) ``` Interestingly, the line `x = a.clone()` is necessary to trigger this error. Please note that this issue happens when using backend `inductor` or `aot_eager`, but does not occur when using backend `eager`. ### Error logs ``` Traceback (most recent call last): File "/workspace/try.py", line 20, in <module> torch.testing.assert_close(res1, res2, equal_nan=True) File "/opt/conda/envs/a3bda49/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/testing/_comparison.py", line 1600, in assert_close raise error_metas[0].to_error(msg) AssertionError: Tensor-likes are not close! Mismatched elements: 2 / 4 (50.0%) Greatest absolute difference: 1.0 at index (0, 1) (up to 1e-05 allowed) Greatest relative difference: 6.563393592834473 at index (0, 1) (up to 1.3e-06 allowed) ``` ### Versions [pip3] numpy==1.26.4 [pip3] optree==0.18.0 [pip3] pytorch-triton==3.3.1+gitc8757738 [pip3] torch==2.11.0a0+gita3bda49 [conda] numpy 1.26.4 pypi_0 pypi [conda] optree 0.18.0 pypi_0 pypi [conda] pytorch-triton 3.3.1+gitc8757738 pypi_0 pypi [conda] torch 2.11.0a0+gita3bda49 pypi_0 pypi cc @bdhirsh @ezyang @chauhang @penguinwu @bobrenjc93 @aorenste
comments_excerpt: In this repro, the function `foo()` is mutating a tensor with overlapping data. This is undefined behavior ([docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.as_strided.html)), because there is a data race to perform the mutation, so you can get different results depending on the kernel that runs, and we end up with a different behavior under eager vs compile. I think it would be reasonable though for us to try to detect and error on this case under compile though, which is better than "different results than eager". @bdhirsh , I tried the same repro from above and here is my observation on the difference between compile and eager. In eager: The overlapping is happening with [0,1] and [1,0]. The in-place add 1 twice at the overlapping. So we see that element to be +2 from the actual value. For example if as_strided gives me [[-2,-1],[-1,2]]. The output will be [[-1,1],[1,2]] In compile: The addition is happening only once so I am getting [[-1,0],[0,2]]. Should we do addition in the overlapping twice or there should be error on this case? I would like to move forward implementing with your suggestion on the same.

title: Incorrect flop count estimate using remat scan
issue_body_excerpt: ### Description This was [originally posted](https://github.com/google/flax/issues/3492) as a Flax issue, but the developers recommended posting here. ### Problem you have encountered: When using flax.linen.remat_scan for constant-time compilation w.r.t. depth, our team is encountering an error in the estimated FLOP count for the compiled training step. In particular, we are observing that the estimated flop count is _lower_ than the product of the batch size per device times the model parameters, which is impossible, since the gradient of the loss must be computed for each example separately, then summed. The issue goes away when using a for-loop to iterate over layers instead, even though the parameter count is verified to be the same for both models. The flop count estimate changes slightly for jit vs pmap, but the issue of a clearly erroneous flop count is only observed when using flax.linen.remat_scan. ### Steps to reproduce: A *minimal example*. ``` from typing import Dict from typing import Tuple from typing import Type import flax.linen as nn import jax import jax.numpy as jnp import optax from absl import app from absl import flags from absl import logging from flax import jax_utils from flax.training import common_utils from flax.training.train_state import TrainState FLAGS = flags.FLAGS flags.DEFINE_boolean("use_remat_scan", True, "Use remat_scan?") BSZ = 8 D_MODEL = 10 D_FF = 40 N_LAYER = 24 class MLP(nn.Module): d_model: int d_ff: int @nn.compact def __call__(self, x): af1 = nn.Dense(self.d_ff)(x) af2 = nn.Dense(self.d_model)(jax.nn.silu(af1)) return x + af2 class StackedMLPsRematted(nn.Module): d_model: int d_ff: int n_layer: int @nn.compact def __call__(self, x): return nn.remat_scan(MLP, lengths=(self.n_layer, 1))( d_model=self.d_model, d_ff=self.d_ff, name="stack", )(x) class StackedMLPsListed(nn.Module): d_model: int d_ff: int n_layer: int @nn.compact def __call__(self, x): for _ in range(self.n_layer): x = MLP(d_model=self.d_model, d_ff=self.d_ff)(x) return x def loss_fn(params, batch, cls): predictions = cls(D_MODEL, D_FF, N_LAYER).apply({"params": params}, batch["inputs"]) loss_terms = optax.l2_loss(targets=batch["targets"], predictions=predictions) loss = jnp.mean(loss_terms) return loss def train_op( train_state: TrainState, batch: Dict[str, jax.Array], is_pmapped: bool, cls: Type[nn.Module], ) -> Tuple[TrainState, jax.Array]: loss, grads = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn)( train_state.params, batch=batch, cls=cls, ) if is_pmapped: loss, grads = jax.lax.pmean([loss, grads], axis_name="devices") return train_state.apply_gradients(grads=grads), loss def get_deterministic_trainstate_and_batch(cls): x = jax.random.normal(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), [BSZ, D_MODEL]) y = jax.random.normal(jax.random.PRNGKey(1), [BSZ, D_MODEL]) batch = dict(inputs=x, targets=y) ps = cls(D_MODEL, D_FF, N_LAYER).init({"params": jax.random.PRNGKey(2)}, x) train_state = TrainState.create( apply_fn=None, params=ps["params"].unfreeze(), tx=optax.sgd(learning_rate=0.01), ) return train_state, batch def pmapped_train_op_cost_analysis(cls): train_state, batch = get_deterministic_trainstate_and_batch(cls) p_train_op = jax.pmap( train_op, axis_name="devices", donate_argnums=(0,), static_broadcasted_argnums=(2, 3), ) compiled = p_train_op.lower( jax_utils.replicate(train_state), common_utils.shard(batch), True, cls, ).compile() cost_analysis = compiled.cost_analysis() return cost_analysis def jitted_train_op_cost_analysis(cls): train_state, cost_analysis = compiled.cost_analysis() return cost_analysis def evaluate_cost_analysis(train_state, cost_analysis): if cost_analysis is not None: n_flop = cost_analysis[0]["flops"] jax.local_device_count() logging.info(f"Example count: {n_example}") n_min_flop_reasonable = n_example * n_param logging.info(f"Reasonable flop count min: {n_min_flop_reasonable}") is_reasonable = n_flop > n_min_flop_reasonable logging.info(f"Is reasonable estimate: {is_reasonable}") def main(argv): del argv cls = StackedMLPsRematted if FLAGS.use_remat_scan else StackedMLPsListed title: [Feature request] Vulkan Target
issue_body_excerpt: I was trying different python parallelization/jit frameworks like jax and taichi, but I am always coming back to Numba due to it being beginner friendly and one can gradually increase the efficiency with further understanding. With that being said, I was a bit sad to see that only CUDA was supported as a GPU backend (now it is managed with a [plugin by nvidia](https://github.com/NVIDIA/numba-cuda) themselves) while the support for AMD (ROCm) was first added and then removed. Supporting all of the platforms would be a huge endeavor for a project like Numba, so a simpler alternative would be great to have. While exploring taichi I discovered that they support multiple "backends", and one of them were OpenGL/Vulkan. While the multiple backends enabled to write one kernel, which could be executed onto multiple platforms, I was more surprised to see OpenGL/Vulkan support, which meant I was kinda platform agnostic, as long as the target platform could setup/run OpenGL/Vulkan. Since OpenGL is a bit older, I was wondering how hard it would be to support Vulkan as a backend for Numba. While the performance would not be on par as using native APIs/frameworks, it would still be a huge benefit and make using different hardware much easier! There has been a comment regarding using the Vulkan LLVM as an intermediate step for Apples Metal API: https://github.com/numba/numba/issues/5706#issuecomment-985233765 I have no experience in such matters, but if someone could give me some hints where to lookup stuff, I could maybe start with a proof of concept!

This will be discussed at the maintainer's meeting today, the result of the discussion will be posted in the meeting notes (follow links from the wiki to them). There would also be a large number of "moving parts" in the toolchain, which may also make such an endeavour more challenging. Were someone or group of persons to show up and want to do this, Numba likely has APIs to help with this task already (as demonstrated by the out-of-tree CUDA target).
