title: [QST] How does cudf perform groupby and aggregation on uint128 types?
issue_body_excerpt: How does cudf perform groupby and aggregation on uint128 types?
comments_excerpt: cuDF only supports 128 bit types for decimal (fixed point) data. Generic 128 bit signed/unsigned integer data types are not supported. See this blog post for information about 128 bit decimals, which are internally represented by the CUDA extension type `__int128`: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/implementing-high-precision-decimal-arithmetic-with-cuda-int128/ @bdice Is there a plan to support it in the future? "128 bit types for decimal" cannot be used for the group by column. Is there any other solution? Currently I don’t think there is a plan for supporting 128 bit integer types. The cost to extend the type matrix is very high due to compile time, and there are a lot of places where 64 bit integers are the maximum width we could support for computation without significant changes to the library’s internals. How is your input data being stored / computed? (Where do the 128 bit types come from?) Do you need this for cuDF Python or some other interface? Side note: I did a little more research and I think the CUDA extended types may only include signed `__int128`. I didn’t see any references to unsigned `__uint128`, so it is unlikely that cuDF could support the unsigned type without new CUDA language features. @bdice The uint128 data comes from the hash calculation of character strings, which improves the GPU computing performance and uses 128 bits to ensure a very low collision probability. Since you don't have to do math on these hash values, you just need to store them, you have some decent options: - You could use a string column with a UTF-8 encoding of the raw binary data (or a plain string encoding of the hexadecimal or decimal integer form of the value, if you wished) - You could use two uint64s in a struct column - You could use two uint64s in a list column - You could use two separate uint64 columns and always group by both keys @bdice Thank you! The struct and list do not support the GroupBy operation in the cudf. Therefore, the two-column uint64 is used. Hello @infzo, thank you for this discussion. Please feel free to reopen if you'd like to revisit this.

title: [BUG] Integer overflow in write_parquet for large tables.
issue_body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** Consider ``` #include <cudf/column/column_factories.hpp> #include <cudf/io/parquet.hpp> #include <cudf/io/types.hpp> #include <cudf/scalar/scalar.hpp> #include <cudf/types.hpp> #include <limits> #include <tuple> int main() { constexpr size_t num_rows = (1L << 31) - 4999; static_assert(num_rows <= std::numeric_limits<cudf::size_type>::max(), "Too many rows"); auto sink = cudf::io::sink_info("foo.pq"); auto val = cudf::numeric_scalar<bool>(true); auto col = cudf::make_column_from_scalar(val, num_rows); auto options = cudf::io::parquet_writer_options::builder( sink, cudf::table_view({col->view()})) .build(); std::ignore = cudf::io::write_parquet(options); return 0; } ``` Which creates a boolean column of _nearly_ `size_type::max()` rows and then attempts to write it to a parquet file. ``` $ ./io-bug [600839][11:34:44:775673][error ] Parquet writer encountered exception during processing. No data has been written to the sink. terminate called after throwing an instance of 'rmm::out_of_memory' what(): std::bad_alloc: out_of_memory: CUDA error (failed to allocate 18446744073692371776 bytes) at: /home/coder/rmm/cpp/include/rmm/mr/device/cuda_memory_resource.hpp:62: cudaErrorMemoryAllocation out of memory Aborted (core dumped) ``` This looks to be due to incorrect use of `div_rounding_up_unsafe` in the parquet writer. When converting the table to parquet data we do: ``` std::vector<int> num_frag_in_part; std::transform(partitions.begin(), partitions.end(), std::back_inserter(num_frag_in_part), [max_page_fragment_size](auto const& part) { return util::div_rounding_up_unsafe(part.num_rows, max_page_fragment_size); }); ``` In this case, `part.num_rows` is $2^{31} - 4999$ and `max_page_fragment_size` is $5000$. `div_rounding_up_unsafe` does `(dividend + divisor - 1) / divisor` which here is $(2^{31} - 4999 + 5000 - 1) / 5000$. But $2^{31} - 4999 + 5000$ overflows the int32 limit and we end up with `num_frag_in_part == -429497` and then when allocate the row_group_fragments we get nonsense. A minimal fix appears to be: ```diff diff --git a/cpp/src/io/parquet/writer_impl.cu b/cpp/src/io/parquet/writer_impl.cu index 621eadb0e5..342f7aeefb 100644 --- a/cpp/src/io/parquet/writer_impl.cu +++ b/cpp/src/io/parquet/writer_impl.cu @@ -1766,7 +1766,7 @@ auto convert_table_to_parquet_data(table_input_metadata& table_meta, partitions.end(), std::back_inserter(num_frag_in_part), [max_page_fragment_size](auto const& part) { - return util::div_rounding_up_unsafe(part.num_rows, max_page_fragment_size); + return util::div_rounding_up_safe<int>(part.num_rows, max_page_fragment_size); }); size_type num_fragments = std::reduce(num_frag_in_part.begin(), num_frag_in_part.end()); ``` But there are a number of other div_rounding_up_unsafe calls in this file which I think should also be audited.

title: Discussion on multi-GPU support for cuFFT and cuSOLVER
issue_body_excerpt: Original context: See #2644. Some of CUDA libraries like cuFFT and cuSOLVER provide native multi-GPU support. However, there is no guarantee that multiple GPUs will outperform single GPU; on the contrary, for cuFFT I found in https://github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/2644#issuecomment-558835428 that any workload that can be handled in one GPU should ***not*** be processed using multi GPUs; the extra data transfer just kills the performance (even if NVLinks are present). I suspect the same holds for cuSOLVER. Since CuPy operations incurs additional memory overhead, I think it is clear that multi-GPU is useful only when the workload is too large to fit in one GPU. For such excessive workloads, it's better/unavoidable to start from NumPy arrays directly, such as the "NumPy-in, NumPy-out" feature currently implemented in #2644. **This thread is for discussions regarding this feature and other possible alternative strategies.**
comments_excerpt: @asi1024 Any chance you've discussed this issue further internally? Thanks. @leofang Sorry for my late response. We are considering that unified memory may be useful for this issue. ([Related issue in stack overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/57752516/how-to-use-cuda-pinned-zero-copy-memory-for-a-memory-mapped-file)) @asi1024 Did you mean ***pinned*** memory or ***unified*** memory? For the former, yes it will benefit the performance of host-device transfer, and it is possible to create a NumPy array from a pinned memory, something like ```python ptr = cp.cuda.alloc_pinned_memory(itemsize*size) np_array = np.frombuffer(ptr, dtype, size).reshape(shape) ``` So the "NumPy-in, NumPy-out" feature will speed up further. The SO post you linked is along this line, with extra effort that the host memory is backed by disk via mmap. For the latter, I don't think it would help. Unified memory allocated via `cudaMallocManaged` is simply for writing CPU/GPU agnostic code and making code porting easier. It does not provide the sought-after optimization: > An important point is that a carefully tuned CUDA program that uses streams and cudaMemcpyAsync to efficiently overlap execution with data transfers may very well perform better than a CUDA program that only uses Unified Memory. > ... > Unified Memory is first and foremost a productivity feature that provides a smoother on-ramp to parallel computing, without taking away any of CUDA’s features for power users. (from https://devblogs.nvidia.com/unified-memory-in-cuda-6/). My understanding for using unified memory is that it would need lots of device synchronization (see the examples therein). you can have a Cupy array living in unified memory, which allows it to be bigger than a single gpu memory size. @emcastillo True, but I don’t think this is supported by cuFFT, and I suspect it’s not supported by cuSOLVER either. For multi-GPU cuFFT the content must live on GPUs in a specified format, which is supposed to be managed by `cufftXtMalloc` but I handled manually in #2644. If unified memory is supported there, it must be an undocumented feature. Update: #2644 is merged, but currently the "NumPy-in, NumPy-out" feature is removed (3e2b7d0 and 705fe1a). We should revisit this in the near future. I still think it is a necessary feature for performance reasons. One more thing: > For multi-GPU cuFFT the content must live on GPUs in a specified format, which is supposed to be managed by cufftXtMalloc but I handled manually in #2644. If unified memory is supported there, it must be an undocumented feature. I think I was wrong about the unified memory. From [the cuFFT doc](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cufft/index.html#accessing-cufft): > Functions in the cuFFT and cuFFTW library assume that the data is in GPU visible memory. This means any memory allocated by cudaMalloc, cudaMallocHost and cudaMallocManaged or registered with cudaHostRegister can be used as input, output or plan work area with cuFFT and cuFFTW functions. For the best performance input data, output data and plan work area should reside in device memory. It seems data managed by the unified memory system can be used, and moreover host data pointer can be passed to cuFFT routines. But we will need to do some performance benchmarks to determine the best strategy. It is also unclear if multi-GPU cuFFT supports unified memory similarly. It's unclear to me if the cuSOLVER can do similar things. Rel: #1429

issue_body_excerpt: `cuda.grid(1)` returns an incorrect value in the following code: ```py import numpy as np from numba import cuda @cuda.jit def bug(out): i = cuda.threadIdx.x + cuda.blockIdx.x * cuda.blockDim.x i2 = cuda.grid(1) if i != i2: # this shouldn't happen print(i, i2) free_mem, _ = cuda.current_context().get_memory_info() # max_num_parallel_iter is around 566281830 on my 4090 max_num_parallel_iter = free_mem // 4 - 128 * 1024 * 1024 dev_out = cuda.device_array(max_num_parallel_iter, dtype=np.float32) bug[22121216, 256](dev_out) ``` One example of a case which is printed is when `i = 2147551327` and `i2 = -214741596`, which likely indicates a signed 32 bit integer overflow. The bug doesn't appear when setting `max_num_parallel_iter` to an integer constant, which must mean it's somehow related to the calculation from the memory info.
comments_excerpt: Thanks for the report! I can reproduce this, and it is due to an integer overflow. > The bug doesn't appear when setting `max_num_parallel_iter` to an integer constant, which must mean it's somehow related to the calculation from the memory info. I think the reason you don't see it is that launches are asynchronous, and setting `max_num_parallel_iter` to a constant changed the timing of execution such that your program manages to exit before the values printed by the kernel get flushed into the terminal. I find that (and I think you should be able to reproduce too) adding `cuda.synchronize()` to the end of the program manifests the error even when there's no computation or device array: ``` from numba import cuda @cuda.jit def bug(): i = cuda.threadIdx.x + cuda.blockIdx.x * cuda.blockDim.x i2 = cuda.grid(1) if i != i2: # this shouldn't happen print(i, i2) bug[22121216, 256]() cuda.synchronize() ``` I have a fix in https://github.com/gmarkall/numba/commit/c40f740c2f9c0831ac1a7d6fada919ce60605bc7 - I will need to add tests to this for a PR, but intend to do this soon. @nathanfarlow There is a fix in PR #9235. As a workaround for now, can you write your kernels such that they don't require more than 2^31 threads, or use the manual computation? One reason what seems like an "obvious" problem has slipped by for so long is that I think people generally don't use so many threads, so this isn't a common pattern in practice. Instead, it's usually more efficient to use a grid-strided loop with fewer threads, as outlined in: https://towardsdatascience.com/cuda-by-numba-examples-1-4-e0d06651612f#0909 Thanks for looking into this and thanks for the advice! :)
